subtitle: Learn what a cultural navigator does, how the role differs from an interpreter, a broker and a case manager, and how to work alongside a navigator so people understand their choices the first time.
audience: For all DHS and DSD staff who meet people at intake, assessment, planning, renewals or complaints, and for anyone curious about the role. It does not create navigator positions, set program rules or replace language access duties.

lessons.title: A bridge between a community and a system
objectives: Describe a cultural navigator as a trusted go-between who helps a person and a service system understand each other.
Name five things navigators commonly do: explain context, go along, connect, build trust and feed back.
Explain why navigation tends to help most when it is tied to a specific step in a process.
Recognize that the person served decides whether a navigator takes part and what is shared.
lessons.teaching:
Many people we serve meet a system that was not built around their language, the way their family makes decisions or what they have lived through with government. A cultural navigator helps close that distance. A navigator is usually a trusted member of a community, or someone who knows it well, who works between that community and a service system. The National Center for Cultural Competence at Georgetown University uses Jezewski's description of cultural brokering, the older name for much of this work: "the act of bridging, linking, or mediating between groups or persons of different cultural backgrounds for the purpose of reducing conflict or producing change."

Programs use different names, but navigators tend to do the same handful of things. They explain context: what a form, letter or question is really asking, and what an answer really means. They go along to assessments, team meetings and appointments. They connect people to providers, benefits and community resources. They build trust by following up and reaching people the system has lost touch with. And they feed back, telling the agency where a process keeps breaking down for a community. California's Department of Social Services describes the same kind of work for child welfare cultural brokers, from linking families with local resources to joining team meetings and appointments.

Navigation tends to help most when it is attached to a specific step. In a 2021 randomized trial in primary care, families of young children who screened positive for autism were offered either family navigation or usual care management. Within a year, 85.7% of children in the navigation group had a diagnostic answer, compared with 76.4% in the comparison group. For Hispanic families the gap was much larger: 90.9% compared with 53.3%. The authors also found that results varied by clinic, so navigation is promising, not a guarantee.

A navigator works with a person, never on them. The person decides whether a navigator takes part, what is shared and who speaks for them. A navigator does not decide eligibility or services. Those responsibilities stay with the staff and offices that hold them, and so does the duty to provide language access.
lessons.keyPoint: A navigator helps a person and a system understand each other at the moments that matter. The person decides whether a navigator joins, and staff keep their own responsibilities.
lessons.example: Practice case: A family was referred for disability services three months ago and has missed two appointments. When the case manager finally reaches the parent by phone, with an interpreter on the line, the parent says they are not sure what the program is or why the county keeps calling. The case manager knows that a community organization nearby offers navigation in the family's language.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do next?
choices: Send the referral to the community organization and ask its navigator to visit the family.
Mail the program brochure again and wait for the family to call back.
Explain the program in plain words, then ask the parent whether they would like help from a navigator, and share contact details only with their agreement.
feedback: This is well meant, but it shares the family's information and sends someone new to their door before they have agreed. The family gets to decide.
A brochure can help, but it repeats what has not worked. The parent has told the case manager that the gap is understanding, not paperwork.
This answers the parent's real question first, offers a navigator as a choice and keeps the family in charge of their own information. Follow your program's rules for any release of information.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time someone helped you through a process that was new to you, such as a hospital stay, a school system or a move. What did that person do that a form or a website could not?
lessons.action: Find out whether your program already works with navigators, cultural brokers or community organizations that offer navigation, and write down how a person would be connected to one.

check.question: Which description best fits a cultural navigator?
check.correct: A trusted go-between who helps a person and a service system understand each other and move through a process.
wrong: A staff member who makes eligibility decisions in the person's language.
Anyone on the team who happens to speak the person's language.
check.feedback: A navigator bridges understanding in both directions and helps a person through a process. Decisions stay with the responsible staff, and speaking a language does not by itself make someone a navigator or an interpreter.

lessons.title: Interpreter, broker, navigator: who does what
objectives: Tell a cultural navigator apart from an interpreter, a cultural broker, a case manager and a community health worker.
Explain why a qualified interpreter is still needed when a navigator who speaks the person's language is present.
Recognize navigation roles that already exist in Minnesota, such as MNsure navigators and community health workers.
Match the helper to what the person actually needs.
lessons.teaching:
An interpreter carries what each person says, accurately and impartially, in both directions. Interpretation is part of an agency's language access duties. A navigator who shares a person's language is not automatically a qualified interpreter, and asking them to interpret pulls them out of their own role. When both are needed, book both: the interpreter carries the words, and the navigator helps the person make sense of the process.

Cultural broker and cultural navigator overlap, and many programs use the names interchangeably. Writing for the National Center for Cultural Competence, Jezewski and Sotnik describe a cultural broker as "a go-between, one who advocates on behalf of another individual or group." Broker programs often stress mediating between a family and an agency and pressing the agency to change. Navigator programs often stress walking one person through one process. What matters more than the name is a clear, written scope, which is the subject of this app's course Cultural Broker as a Role.

A case manager holds responsibility for a person's plan and services. A navigator supports the person in understanding and taking part, and does not replace the case manager. Minnesota also has navigation roles you may meet. MNsure-certified navigators give free help applying for, enrolling in and renewing Medical Assistance and MinnesotaCare, and they work through community organizations. Community health workers are recognized in Minnesota Health Care Programs: the Minnesota Department of Health notes coverage of their health education since 2009 and of Community Health Integration services, which include system navigation, since 2024.

To choose well, start with what the person needs. If they cannot follow the words, they need an interpreter. If they follow the words but not what the process means, what their choices are or why they should trust it, a navigator may help. If the question is health coverage, a MNsure navigator may be the right door. Often the answer is more than one helper, each in their own role.
lessons.keyPoint: The interpreter carries the words. The navigator helps the person make sense of the process. The case manager holds the plan. When more than one is needed, give each person their own role.
lessons.example: Practice case: The newer colleague is scheduling an assessment. The person's family has asked that a navigator from their community come along. The newer colleague tells the case manager that the navigator speaks the family's language, so there is no need to book an interpreter.
lessons.question: What should the case manager suggest?
choices: Agree. The navigator can interpret and support the family at the same time.
Book a qualified interpreter and welcome the navigator as the family's support.
Tell the family the navigator cannot come because the assessment is confidential.
feedback: This blurs two roles. The navigator may not be a qualified interpreter, and while interpreting they cannot also support the family. The family loses the help they asked for.
This gives each person their own role. The interpreter carries the words accurately, and the navigator can focus on helping the family understand and take part.
The person can choose who joins them. Confidentiality is handled through consent and your program's rules, not by turning away the support the family asked for.
lessons.reflection: Where in your own work could a person understand every word and still not understand what is happening or what their choices are?
lessons.action: Write three short lines in your own words: what an interpreter does, what a navigator does and what you do. Keep them where you prepare for meetings with the people you serve.

check.question: A navigator who speaks the family's language joins an assessment. Who should interpret?
check.correct: A qualified interpreter, so the navigator can focus on supporting the family.
wrong: The navigator, since they already speak the language.
A family member, since the family knows the person best.
check.feedback: Interpretation is a language access duty and calls for a qualified interpreter. A navigator or a relative who speaks the language is there for other reasons, and asking them to interpret changes their role.

lessons.title: Where culture changes the answer
objectives: Identify the points in disability services where culture can change what a question or an answer means.
Describe how a navigator can help an assessor or case manager read an answer in context.
Connect this work to Minnesota's informed decision-making law, which names a person's cultural needs.
Check what an answer means before it becomes part of a plan.
lessons.teaching:
Some moments in services carry more weight than others: first contact, assessment, choosing services, services starting, renewals and raising a concern. At each one, a misunderstanding can change what a person receives. A family may not call back because they do not know what the program offers. A question about independence or about who helps at home can be heard differently from how it was meant. Options can be listed without being understood. A missed letter can end coverage.

Minnesota law names culture directly. For people on disability waivers, Minnesota Statutes, section 256B.4905, subdivision 3a, says informed decision making must include "identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers." A navigator is one good way to meet that expectation. It is not the only way, and the responsibility stays with the staff who hold the plan.

Here is how a misreading happens. Asked who helps at home, a parent says, "Family takes care of family." That can mean relatives are there every day. It can also mean relatives help when they can around work, or that the family does not want to seem unable to cope in front of someone from the county. Written down as "needs met by family," it can shrink a plan. A navigator can help the family understand why the question is asked, and help staff ask the follow-up that gets to the real answer.

The skill for every staff member is the same with or without a navigator. Notice when an answer could mean more than one thing, and check before you write it down. Ask about specific hours, tasks and what happens when a helper is not available. With the person's agreement, you can also ask a navigator whether anything about how a question was asked might have been heard differently. Ask about this conversation, not about what a whole community believes.
lessons.keyPoint: When an answer could mean more than one thing, check before it becomes part of a plan. A navigator can help you ask the follow-up that finds the real answer.
lessons.example: Practice case: During an assessment, the assessor asks who helps the person at home. The person's mother answers through the interpreter, "We all help. Family takes care of family." The assessor begins to note that daily help is covered. The navigator, sitting with the family, asks the mother whether she wants to mention her schedule. She nods, and explains through the interpreter that she works nights and that the family did not want to seem unable to cope.
lessons.question: What should the assessor do?
choices: Note that family support covers daily help, since that is what the mother said first.
Ask the navigator to answer the rest of the support questions, since they understand the family.
Thank the mother and the navigator, then ask the family about specific hours, tasks and what happens on the nights she works.
feedback: The first answer was sincere, but the family has now shown it was not the whole picture. Recording only the first answer could leave the person without help on the nights that matter.
The navigator can explain context, but the family speaks for itself. Answers about the person's support need to come from the person and the family.
This welcomes the new information, keeps the family as the source of their own answers and gets the specific details a fair plan needs.
lessons.reflection: Which question in your own work is most likely to be heard differently from how you mean it? What follow-up question would help?
lessons.action: Pick one question you ask often. Write one specific follow-up you can use when an answer could mean more than one thing, such as asking about particular hours or tasks.

check.question: For people on disability waivers, what does Minnesota's informed decision-making law say the process must include?
check.correct: Identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers.
wrong: A cultural navigator at every assessment.
A cultural score for each person, recorded in the plan.
check.feedback: Minnesota Statutes, section 256B.4905, subdivision 3a, names cultural needs and culturally responsive services and providers. A navigator is one way to meet that, not a legal requirement, and the law does not call for scoring anyone's culture.

lessons.title: Working alongside a navigator
objectives: Respect the person's choice about whether a navigator takes part, who it is and what is shared.
Treat navigation as a defined role, not extra work quietly added to a bilingual coworker's job.
Agree on roles before a meeting and close the loop with the navigator afterward.
Pass on what navigators notice about forms, letters and processes so the system can improve.
lessons.teaching:
Start with the person. Ask whether they would like a navigator rather than assuming they would. Some people want someone from their own community, and some would rather not, for reasons of privacy or trust. Share information only with the person's agreement and within your program's privacy rules. If they say no, that is their answer, and you still owe them a clear explanation in a language they understand.

Navigation is a role, not a favor. Programs that use navigators and brokers well make it a real job. M Health Fairview, for example, has had cultural brokers since 2016 who spend much of their time at trusted community organizations. A study of a Virginia family support program by Pang and Yarbrough recommends that providers work with families to decide what brokers do and how support is offered. Asking a bilingual coworker to "just come along" on top of their own caseload is different. It adds work nobody counts, and it can leave that coworker caught between their community and their job. The course Cultural Broker as a Role covers how to name and scope this work.

Before a meeting, agree on who does what: who explains the program, who interprets, who supports the family and who makes decisions. During the meeting, speak to the person, not to the navigator. A navigator is not the family's spokesperson and not the agency's messenger.

After the meeting, close the loop. With the person's agreement, let the navigator know what happens next so they are not left guessing. And when a navigator tells you a letter confuses people, or a step loses families, pass it on to someone who can change it. That is the feedback part of the role, and it is how one family's experience can make the process better for the next.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask the person first, give everyone a clear role and close the loop afterward. What a navigator notices about a process is information the agency can use.
lessons.example: Practice case: The supervisor notices several stalled cases with families who share a language with one of the team's case managers. The program manager suggests asking that case manager to join those visits and help families understand the process, in addition to their own caseload.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do?
choices: Ask the case manager to do it. It is only a few visits, and the families need help.

Talk with the case manager about what they are willing to do, treat it as real work by adjusting their caseload or connecting families with a community navigator, and raise the pattern with the program manager.
Say no, to protect the case manager's time, and leave the cases as they are.
feedback: The need is real, but this adds uncounted work to one person and treats a language skill as a favor. It can also strain the case manager's place in their own community.

This respects the case manager, treats navigation as work that counts and looks for a lasting answer for the families. Raising the pattern helps the program see that the need is bigger than a few visits.
This protects the case manager, but the families stay stuck. Saying no to one solution is a start; the cases still need another way forward.
lessons.reflection: Have you ever been asked, or asked someone, to help with work outside the job because of a language or a background? What would have made it fair?
lessons.action: The next time you work with a navigator, take two minutes before the meeting to agree on who explains, who interprets and who decides, and two minutes afterward to agree on what happens next.

check.question: Which step best respects the person served when a navigator might help?
check.correct: Ask the person whether they would like a navigator and what they are comfortable sharing.
wrong: Bring a navigator from the person's community to every meeting.
Share the full case file with the navigator so they are fully prepared.
check.feedback: The person decides whether a navigator takes part, who it is and what is shared. Assuming someone from their community is wanted, or sharing more than they agreed to, takes that choice away.

cards.back: A trusted go-between who helps a person and a service system understand each other and move through a process.
Carries what each person says, accurately and impartially, in both directions. A language access duty, separate from navigation.
A closely related role that mediates between a family and an agency and often presses the agency to change. Many programs use the names interchangeably.
A step where a misunderstanding changes what a person receives, such as first contact, assessment, informed choice, renewal or a complaint.
Checking what an answer means before it becomes part of a plan, by asking about specific hours, tasks and situations.
Real, defined and counted work, not a favor added to a bilingual coworker's caseload.

aid.heading: When a navigator might help
items: The person follows the words but not what the process means or what their choices are.
Calls go unanswered, appointments are missed or letters are not acted on.
The person or family asks for someone from their community.
Trust in the agency seems low, or past experiences with government come up.
An important step is coming: assessment, choosing services, a renewal or a complaint.

aid.heading: Before the meeting
items: Ask the person whether they would like a navigator, and who.
Agree on what the person is comfortable sharing, and follow your program's rules for any release.
Book a qualified interpreter separately when one is needed.
Agree on roles: who explains, who interprets, who supports and who decides.

aid.heading: During the meeting
items: Speak to the person, not to the navigator.
When an answer could mean more than one thing, ask about specific hours, tasks and situations.
Welcome context from the navigator, and let the person give their own answers.

aid.heading: After the meeting
items: With the person's agreement, tell the navigator what happens next.
Write down any form, letter or step that caused confusion, and pass it to someone who can change it.
If a coworker is doing navigation on top of their job, raise it with your supervisor so the work is counted.

sources.title: National Center for Cultural Competence, Georgetown University — What Is the Role of Cultural Brokers in Health Care Delivery?
sources.note: Source for Jezewski's 1990 definition of cultural brokering and Jezewski and Sotnik's 2001 description of a cultural broker as a go-between, both quoted on this page.

sources.title: Feinberg and others — Effect of Family Navigation on Diagnostic Ascertainment Among Children at Risk for Autism: A Randomized Clinical Trial From DBPNet, JAMA Pediatrics (2021)
sources.note: Randomized trial at 11 urban primary care sites in three cities, 249 families analyzed. Diagnostic answer within one year: 85.7% with family navigation and 76.4% with conventional care management; Hispanic families 90.9% and 53.3%. The authors report that ethnicity and site changed the size of the effect.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 2025, section 256B.4905 — Home and Community-Based Services Policy Statement
sources.note: Subdivision 3a, Informed decision making, applies to people using waiver services under sections 256B.092 and 256B.49 and lists what the process must address, including "identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers."

sources.title: California Department of Social Services — Cultural Broker Resources
sources.note: Describes what child welfare cultural brokers do, including linking families with local resources, assisting with team meetings, attending appointments and court, and home visits.

sources.title: MNsure — Find a Navigator
sources.note: MNsure-certified navigators give free help with applications, enrollment and renewals, with a focus on Medical Assistance and MinnesotaCare, and work through community organizations.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Health — Community Health Worker Initiatives: CHW Employer Toolkit
sources.note: Notes that Minnesota Health Care Programs have covered diagnosis-related health education by community health workers since 2009, and Community Health Integration services, which include system navigation, since 2024. General information, not billing advice.

sources.title: M Health Fairview — Celebrating the M Health Fairview cultural brokers program (January 2023)
sources.note: Describes a Twin Cities cultural broker program working since 2016 with Karen, Hmong, Latine, African American and Native American communities, largely from trusted community organizations.

sources.title: Yali Pang and Dana V. Yarbrough — The Promising Practice of Cultural Brokering Support with Culturally Diverse Families of Children with Developmental Disabilities, Developmental Disabilities Network Journal (2023)
sources.note: Mixed-methods study of a Virginia family-to-family program. Parents rated the cultural brokering service highly; the authors recommend that providers work closely with families to decide brokers' roles and how support is offered.
